claims.text: Google SRE defines five AI autonomy levels: L0 Manual, L1 Assisted, L2 Partial, L3 High, and L4 Full, based on whether automation or humans handle Monitor, Investigate, Mitigate, Actuate, and Self Direct.
At Google SRE autonomy level L2 (Partial), the system can monitor, investigate and actuate, but a human must explicitly approve any plan before actuation.

At Google SRE autonomy level L3 (High), the AI agent can detect, decide and act without human approval for bounded, well-defined scenarios, with humans often notified and safety relying heavily on technical controls and guardrails.

At Google SRE autonomy level L4 (Full), a system devises and executes action sequences, monitors the impact of its interventions, adapts strategy (alternative mitigations or rollbacks), and manages the incident until the system is confirmed stable.

The transition from Google's L2 to L3 is described as a critical step gated by trust and robust safety controls, requiring demonstrated high precision and reliability; the transition from L3 to L4 is gated by the ability to perform Multi-Step Resolution.
Google SRE's AI-Ops governance model, the 'Safety Trifecta', consists of Transparency, Real-time Risk Evaluation, and Progressive Authorization.

Google's Real-time Risk Evaluation assesses every agent-proposed action against production context such as ongoing deployments, error budget status, active incidents and time of day; draining a cell may be low-risk normally but high-risk during a regional peak.
Google requires agent identities to be distinct from human users, strongly authenticated, and granted access only on-demand with necessary permissions (no ambient access, least privilege).
Google requires agent-specific rate limits and automated circuit breakers to prevent runaway loops, and requires any agent action to be highly interruptible.
Google requires any system or API intended for agent interaction to support a declarative dry_run=true mode so the outcome and blast radius can be predicted before production state is mutated.

Google's zero-trust, safe-by-default actuation requires agents to route actions such as draining a cell through a delegated control plane that deterministically verifies available capacity and enforces global rate limits, regardless of whether the caller is an agent or a human.
Google's paper names its autonomous mitigation agent 'AI Operator', its execution guardrail control plane 'Actus', and its incident-trajectory analysis and evaluation system 'IRM Analyzer'.

Google evaluates agents with datasets graded Bronze (heuristic autolabelers), Silver (programmatic, calibrated against Gold) and Gold (human-expert verified), using stratified sampling of incidents for manual review to create Gold data.

Google runs Nightly Evaluations on its Everest platform against a rolling dataset of recent real incidents, combining LLM-as-a-Judge grading of reasoning and tool calls with strict deterministic scoring of the final mitigation.

Google scores a mitigation as correct only if the agent's output deterministically matches the exact parameters of the Golden data (e.g., the specific binary and version), not a vague suggestion to 'rollback'.

Google collects Golden labels inside the incident workflow: when an oncaller declares an incident mitigated, the system suggests the exact mitigations applied and the SRE accepts, modifies or rejects them.

Google's Detectr is a Gemini-powered platform for incident detection, and Google notes LLMs can cluster customer feedback from support tickets and forums in near real-time to identify emerging outages missed by telemetry-based monitoring.
Google's agents begin at Level 2 autonomy, where they investigate, propose and stage mitigations but need explicit human approval to execute, and advance to Level 3 or 4 only later.

PagerDuty's SRE agent Paige runs detect, triage, diagnose, remediate and learn stages; in diagnosis it tests multiple hypotheses in parallel against logs, metrics and code, and it pulls change events, runbooks and observability data as context.
PagerDuty's Paige waits for human approval before every remediation unless the user decides Paige can act independently, and shows the recommendation, reasoning and evidence before execution.
In PagerDuty's example, Paige identified a payments-api v2.4.1 deployment as root cause with 91% confidence and proposed reverting to the last stable version, awaiting approval.
PagerDuty plans per-team agent profiles and permissions (Early Access) to define which integrations and actions Paige can access, and states its releases are tested against prompt injection.

PagerDuty's Paige can be added to an escalation policy or as a virtual responder, can attempt a fix before escalating, and after incidents writes post-incident reviews, updates runbooks and stores shared agent memory.

Traversal's self-healing opens a draft pull request, runs validation checks (unit tests, staging error rate), merges and rolls out, then verifies in production by comparing checkout conversion to its 7-day baseline and confirming all storefronts completed price refresh.

Traversal lets users grant autonomy incrementally per fix type and scope: in its example, cart-svc region and validation fallback fixes run on their own after staging checks pass, while pricing-service code changes still arrive as PRs and pricing-service config rollbacks were later added to autonomous.
